name: Atahualpa
info: Atahualpa (c. 1502–1533), Atawallpa in Quechua, was the last effective Inca emperor, who won the throne from his half-brother Huáscar in a civil war and was captured at Cajamarca and executed by Francisco Pizarro's Spaniards.

facts.born: c. 1502, place disputed: Cusco by the chroniclers Cieza de León and Betanzos, Caranqui or Quito by other accounts and by his own statement before his death; son of the emperor Huayna Cápac
facts.died: 1533 at Cajamarca, garroted by the Spaniards after a trial that sentenced him to be burned; the date is given both as 26 July and as 29 August
facts.role: Governor of Quito under Huáscar; leader of the northern side in the Inca Civil War (1529–1532); Sapa Inca from April 1532, with the regnal name Caccha Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui Inca; a prisoner of the Spaniards from November 1532
facts.known: the Inca Civil War against Huáscar; the victory at Quipaipán and the taking of Cusco; his capture in the ambush at Cajamarca; the room he offered to fill with gold and silver; his trial and execution; the Inkarri myth of his return

t: A son of Huayna Cápac who spent his youth campaigning with his father in the north, Atahualpa governed Quito under his half-brother Huáscar until their rivalry broke into civil war in 1529.
His generals Quizquiz, Chalcuchímac and Rumiñawi won the war in April 1532, capturing Huáscar and seizing Cusco, just as Francisco Pizarro's small Spanish force was marching inland.

Seized in an ambush at Cajamarca in November 1532, he offered a room of gold and silver for his life, but the Spaniards tried him for revolt, idolatry and Huáscar's murder and garroted him in 1533 after his baptism.
dyk: The Quechua word wallpa for 'chicken' was long thought to explain Atahualpa's name; since the bird was new to the Andes, scholars now think it more likely the bird was named after him, as Blas Valera said in the 16th century.
ev: Born a son of the Inca emperor Huayna Cápac, in Cusco by the most trusted chronicles, though other accounts place his birth near Quito
Relations with Huáscar have broken down, and the two brothers begin the Inca Civil War over the succession
Francisco Pizarro lands on Puná Island with 180 men and 37 horses and hears of the civil war
His generals defeat Huáscar's army at Quipaipán in April, capture Huáscar and seize Cusco
Captured in November in an ambush on the square at Cajamarca, where the Spaniards kill a great number of his retinue
Condemned by a trial staged by Pizarro, baptised to escape burning and executed by garrote

sections.early:
Atahualpa, Atawallpa in Quechua, was born around the turn of the 16th century, about 1502, a son of the Inca emperor Huayna Cápac. His birthplace and mother are disputed. Pedro Cieza de León, who questioned the Inca nobility of Cusco, wrote that he was born in Cusco to Tuto Palla, a woman from the Quito region, and Juan de Betanzos that his mother was an Inca princess of the line of Pachacuti. In the 18th century Juan de Velasco made him the son of a princess of a Kingdom of Quito, a version historians such as Raúl Porras Barrenechea have rejected for want of evidence. Most Peruvian historians follow the chroniclers who place his birth in Cusco and hold that Huáscar's partisans spread the Quito story to brand him a usurper; some Ecuadorian historians favour Quito or Caranqui.

He spent his childhood with his father in Cusco and passed through the Warachikuy, the rite that marked the passage to adulthood. When he was thirteen the Caranquis and Cayambis rose in the north, and he went with his father and his brother Ninan Cuyuchi at the head of the army to the Quito region, while Huáscar was among the governors left in Cusco. For more than ten years he helped his father put down rebellions and conquer new lands, with the support of the generals Chalcuchímac and Quizquiz, and learned the work of government. The chroniclers described him as someone of 'lively reasoning and with great authority'.
sections.rise:
Huayna Cápac and his chosen successor, Ninan Cuyuchi, died in a smallpox epidemic around 1525; elsewhere the father's death is given as 1527. Atahualpa at first accepted his half-brother Huáscar as emperor, and Huáscar made him governor of Quito. Huáscar saw him as the greatest threat to his power but, out of respect for their father's wishes, did not remove him. During a tense peace Huáscar won the support of the Cañari, a powerful people of the north who bore grudges against Atahualpa from his father's campaigns, while Atahualpa sought to build an independent state in Quito. By 1529 relations had broken down.

According to the chronicler Pedro Pizarro, an army sent by Huáscar ambushed and captured Atahualpa at Tumebamba; he escaped, having lost an ear, and afterwards wore a headpiece fastened under his chin to hide it. Miguel Cabello de Balboa thought the story improbable, since Huáscar's men would have killed him at once. Atahualpa raised a great army in Quito, levelled Tumebamba and the lands around it, and was wounded in the leg in an attack by raft on the island of Puná. After a defeat by Huáscar's general Atoc at Chillopampa, his generals regrouped, defeated Atoc at Mulliambato, and tortured and killed him. As he advanced slowly on Cusco, an oracle of the huaca Catequil foretold that his advance would end badly; he killed its priest and had the temple destroyed.
sections.deeds:
Atahualpa's leading generals, Quizquiz, Chalcuchímac and Rumiñawi, won the war for him. In April 1532 they were victorious at Mullihambato, Chimborazo and finally Quipaipán, the last battle between the brothers. Quizquiz and Chalcuchímac defeated Huáscar's army, captured Huáscar, killed his family and seized the capital, Cusco. Atahualpa's reign as Sapa Inca is counted from that April, under the regnal name Caccha Pachacuti Inca Yupanqui Inca, taken from the caccha idol and in honour of the emperor Pachacuti. He himself had stayed in the Andean city of Cajamarca with an army of about 80,000.

It was there that he learned that strangers were advancing into the empire. Francisco Pizarro had landed on Puná in January 1531 with 180 men and 37 horses, occupied Tumbes, which the islanders of Puná had ruined, and heard of the civil war. In September 1532 he founded San Miguel de Piura and marched inland with 106 foot soldiers and 62 horsemen. Atahualpa sent a noble who spent two days in the Spanish camp assessing their weapons and horses. Judging that 168 men were no threat to his 80,000, he invited them to Cajamarca, expecting to capture them, and let them cross difficult country unopposed. They reached the town on 15 November 1532 and Pizarro sent Hernando de Soto and then Hernando Pizarro to his camp near the hot springs, where he agreed to visit them the next day.
sections.opponents:
Pizarro prepared an ambush, hiding his cavalry and infantry in three long buildings on the square and placing musketeers and four pieces of artillery in a stone structure in its middle. Atahualpa entered late the next afternoon in a litter carried by eighty lords, with 5,000 to 6,000 men carrying small battle axes, slings and stones under their clothes; one account says he was very drunk. Only the Dominican friar Vincente de Valverde came out, with an interpreter. Accounts of what Valverde said differ, but eyewitnesses agree that he spoke of the Catholic faith; Atahualpa demanded the return of everything the Spaniards had taken, examined the breviary he was handed and threw it to the ground. At Pizarro's signal the Spaniards charged, killing a great number of the Inca's retinue while the rest fled; Pizarro took Atahualpa only after killing all who carried his litter. No Spaniard died.

Atahualpa's own conduct in the war was harsh: his generals tortured and killed Atoc and killed Huáscar's family, and he killed Catequil's priest. While a captive he also arranged the execution of Huáscar, a killing the Spaniards later used against him. His enemies, for their part, shaped the record: most Peruvian historians hold that Huáscar's side invented his Quito birth to present him to the Spaniards as a usurper and a bastard, and Rostworowski argues that chroniclers wrongly judged his claim by European rules, since the Inca succession did not rest on primogeniture alone but also on the ability to command.
sections.last:
On 17 November 1532 the Spaniards sacked the Inca camp and found great treasures of gold, silver and emeralds. Seeing their desire for precious metals, Atahualpa offered to fill a room about 6.7 metres long and 5.2 metres wide to a height of 2.4 metres once with gold and twice with silver within two months. It is commonly believed he offered this ransom for his freedom; the historian Hemming writes that he did so to save his life, and none of the early chroniclers mention any Spanish promise to free him once it was paid.

After several months in fear of an attack by the general Rumiñawi, the outnumbered Spaniards came to see their prisoner as too great a liability. Pizarro staged a trial that found him guilty of revolting against the Spaniards, practising idolatry and murdering Huáscar, and sentenced him to be burned at the stake. Atahualpa was horrified, for the Inca believed that a soul could not pass to the afterlife if the body were burned. When Valverde told him that conversion would let the friar persuade Pizarro to change the sentence, he agreed to be baptised. On the morning of his death he told his captors he had been born at Caranqui, in what the Incas called the Kingdom of Quito. He was strangled with a garrote, the account of the execution says on 26 July 1533; his clothes and some of his skin were burned and his remains given a Christian burial. His brother Túpac Huallpa succeeded him, and then another brother, Manco Inca.
sections.legacy:
Atahualpa's death came in the course of the Spanish conquest of the Inca Empire. A line of successors went on claiming the title of emperor, as Spanish vassals or as rebel leaders, but none held comparable power. His favourite sister, Quispe Sisa, whom he had given to Pizarro in marriage, bore Pizarro a daughter, Francisca Pizarro Yupanqui, who was legitimised by imperial decree and married her uncle Hernando Pizarro in Spain.

Among indigenous peoples a myth of his death and future return, the Inkarri, became widespread, recorded as far south as the Huilliche of southern Chile; in a rare Mapuche version recorded by Tom Dillehay he kills the conquistador Pedro de Valdivia. His burial place is unknown. The historian Tamara Estupiñán argues that his remains were taken for safekeeping to a site in Ecuador called Malqui-Machay, where stone walls and underground water canals have been found, though more excavation would be needed to confirm it. Quito's main football stadium bears his name, his statue stands with Moctezuma II's on the façade of the Royal Palace of Madrid among the kings of the realms that formed Spain, and his conflict with Pizarro is the subject of Peter Shaffer's play The Royal Hunt of the Sun (1964).

summary: Atahualpa, a son of Huayna Cápac, defeated his half-brother Huáscar in the Inca Civil War and became Sapa Inca in April 1532. Months later he was captured by Francisco Pizarro's few Spaniards in an ambush at Cajamarca, paid a vast ransom in gold and silver, and was tried and garroted in 1533, the last Inca emperor to hold real power.

notes: Death date conflicts in the article: lead '29 August 1533', the execution section '26 July 1533'; the lead also says 'after his baptism in July 1533, he was garroted'. Year 1533 is firm; day left out of the events and both mentioned in the facts.
Huayna Cápac's death: 'around 1525' in the lead, '1527' in the Pre-conquest section; both given.
Ransom: the lead says 'in exchange for a promise of release'; the body says none of the early chroniclers mention any commitment to free him (Hemming: to save his life). Followed the body.
The 'very drunk' remark is a quotation in the article with no named source; told as 'one account says'.
Hemming and Rostworowski are named without first names, as the article names them.

The article lists presidents among the descendants of an 'Inés' without saying who she is (presumably Quispe Sisa); left out. The article does not say how much of the ransom was actually delivered; left out.
The article is fairly short; 'legacy' leans on descendants and the Inkarri myth because there is no historians' assessment section.
